Variance explained by sample covariates

Source: R/pca_plots.R
plot_variance_explained.Rd

Shows how much of the variation in a dataset each sample covariate (condition, batch, sex, library size, ...) explains, in one of two views:

"genes"

The share of each feature's variance explained by each covariate: one violin (with a box of the quartiles and median) per covariate, ordered by median, Residuals last; or, for a few `features`, stacked bars. From the result of variancePartition::fitExtractVarPartModel(), or computed here with linear models (see Details).

"pcs"

The R-squared of each of the top PCs regressed on each covariate, as tiles under bars of each PC's % variance: which covariates drive the main axes of variation.

Fixed sizes; save it with save_plot; the values behind it are returned by export_source_data.

Usage

plot_variance_explained(
  x,
  metadata = NULL,
  covariates = NULL,
  view = c("genes", "pcs"),
  n.top = NULL,
  n.pcs = 10,
  features = NULL,
  cols = NULL,
  italic.genes = TRUE,
  cell.width = 0.4,
  cell.height = 0.25,
  panel.width = 3,
  panel.height = 2,
  legend.position = "right",
  bg = "transparent"
)

Arguments

x

A normalized features x samples matrix or data frame (e.g. vst, logCPM), sample names as column names; or, for view "genes", a variancePartition result (features x components, with a `Residuals` column); or, for view "pcs", a prcomp result

metadata

Data frame of sample covariates, sample names as row names. Not needed for a variancePartition result

covariates

Columns of `metadata` to use. If NULL (default), all

view

"genes" (default) or "pcs"

n.top

Number of most variable features used from a matrix. If NULL (default): all features for view "genes", 500 for view "pcs" (as plot_pca)

n.pcs

View "pcs": number of PCs, default 10

features

View "genes": features to draw as stacked bars instead of violins (e.g. a few genes of interest). Default is NULL

cols

Colours of the covariates: NULL (default; "scanpy-20"), a qualitative palette name, or colours named by covariate (Residuals are always grey). For view "pcs", the colours of the R-squared scale: NULL (default; "seq-blue"), a palette name or colours from low to high

italic.genes

Whether feature names (stacked bars) are gene names, set in italics. Default is TRUE

cell.width

Width of one violin (view "genes") or one PC column (view "pcs") in inches, default 0.4

cell.height

Height of one bar (stacked bars) or one covariate row (view "pcs") in inches, default 0.25

panel.width

Length of the stacked bars in inches, default 3

panel.height

Height of the violins in inches, default 2

legend.position

Position of the legend (stacked bars and view "pcs"), default "right"

bg

Background colour, default is "transparent"

Value

A ggplot object, or a patchwork for view "pcs"

Details

Built-in fractions (view "genes" from a matrix). For each feature, a linear model of its values on all covariates is fitted (numeric covariates as they are, others as factors), and its R-squared is split between the covariates by the LMG method (Lindeman, Merenda & Gold 1980; as relaimpo::calc.relimp(type = "lmg"), Groemping 2006): a covariate's fraction is its increase in R-squared when added to the model, averaged over all orders in which the covariates can be added. Residuals is 1 - R-squared, so the fractions of a feature sum to 1, as variancePartition's, and do not depend on the order of `covariates`. Variance shared by correlated covariates (e.g. a batch partly confounded with condition) is split between them; fully confounded covariates cannot be separated and give an error. This is an approximation of variancePartition: fixed effects only. With few samples, a covariate with many levels is overfitted; use variancePartition, with such covariates as random effects, for those designs. At most 8 covariates.

View "pcs". Each PC's scores are regressed on each covariate separately (R-squared of a one-covariate linear model; for a factor, the share of the PC's variance between its levels). The source data also hold the F-test p-value and its Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment over all tiles; with few samples they are rough.

See also

plot_pca, save_plot

Examples

set.seed(1)
m <- matrix(rnorm(1000 * 12, mean = 6), nrow = 1000,
            dimnames = list(paste0("Gene", 1:1000), paste0("S", 1:12)))
meta <- data.frame(condition = rep(c("WT", "KO"), each = 6),
                   batch = rep(c("A", "B", "C"), 4),
                   row.names = colnames(m))
m[1:300, meta$condition == "KO"] <- m[1:300, meta$condition == "KO"] + 1.5
m[, meta$batch == "B"] <- m[, meta$batch == "B"] + rnorm(1000, sd = 0.5)
plot_variance_explained(m, meta)

plot_variance_explained(m, meta, features = c("Gene1", "Gene2", "Gene900"))

plot_variance_explained(m, meta, view = "pcs")
#> PCA of 500 features x 12 samples
